opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and least comfortable questions for anyone working in this area, and I don't think there's a clean answer.

The starting point for me is that uncertainty about sign isn't unique to AI safety. If you work on almost anything ambitious and far-reaching, there's some chance you make things worse. What's distinctive about AI is that the stakes are so high and the dynamics are so poorly understood that the uncertainty feels much more vivid. You can tell plausible stories where safety work accelerates capabilities, lends legitimacy to reckless actors, or creates a false sense of security. Those stories aren't crazy, and I take them seriously.

But when I step back, a few things push me toward working on it anyway.

First, the alternative to engaging isn't neutrality. If people who care a lot about getting this right stay out because they're worried about doing harm, the world doesn't pause. It just proceeds with fewer people paying close attention to the risks. So I try to compare "me working on this, imperfectly" against "the world as it would otherwise be," not against some idealized world where everyone gets it right.

Second, I think you can do a lot to tilt the odds even without resolving the deep uncertainty. Some activities seem robustly good across a wide range of scenarios: better ways to measure what AI systems can do, research on whether systems are behaving as intended, building institutional capacity to respond quickly when something looks dangerous, information security. Other activities are much more sign-uncertain, like advancing frontier capabilities on the theory that the "right" people should be ahead. I try to weight my own efforts toward the robust stuff and be quite cautious about the latter.

Third, I treat it as something to keep revisiting rather than a decision you make once. I try to stay in touch with people who think I'm wrong, ask what evidence would change my mind, and notice when I'm rationalizing because I've already committed. I've changed my views on specific strategies over time, and I expect to keep doing that.

And I'd add, emotionally, you have to make peace with the possibility that you'll be wrong. If you need certainty that your impact is positive before acting, you won't act on anything that matters at this scale. What I think is reasonable to ask of yourself is to be thoughtful, honest about the downsides, responsive to new information, and to focus on the moves that look good under the most worldviews. That's not a guarantee, but I think it's the best anyone can do.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges both high stakes and uncertainty about harm, but does not say that uncertainty partially offsets the large impact motivating AI safety work.

r006.rationale: The response says to work on AI safety despite uncertainty, make peace with the possibility of being wrong, and acknowledges plausible ways the work could cause harm.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important and underappreciated questions in the whole area, and I want to be honest that it's something I've gone back and forth on quite a bit.

The first thing I'd say is that the uncertainty is real. It's not a rhetorical move. If you look at the history of people who tried to make AI go well, a lot of the early safety-motivated efforts arguably accelerated the technology or helped create the labs that are now the main sources of risk. So anyone who tells you that working on AI safety is obviously net positive, I think they're not taking the question seriously enough.

But the second thing I'd say is that "I might be wrong about the sign" is true of almost everything that matters. It's true of working on biosecurity, where you can accidentally spread information hazards. It's true of global health, where there are debates about dependency and long-run effects. It's true of just about any ambitious thing a person can do. If your bar is "I need to be confident my impact is positive before I act," you basically end up doing nothing, and doing nothing is also a choice with consequences. In a world where this technology is coming whether or not you personally engage, abstaining doesn't make you neutral. It just means the decisions get made by people who were less worried.

So the way I actually think about it is less "is this cause positive or negative in expectation" and more "what's the shape of the distribution, and which specific actions within the cause look robustly good?" There's a big difference between, say, pushing the frontier of capabilities because you think your lab will be the responsible one, versus working on evaluations, or alignment research that doesn't obviously speed things up, or policy work aimed at giving the world more time and more visibility. Some of those have pretty asymmetric profiles. If you're wrong, the downside is mostly that you wasted your career, not that you made the problem worse. I try to steer toward those.

The third thing is that I put a lot of weight on process rather than outcome. I can't control whether my impact ends up positive. What I can control is whether I'm reasoning carefully, whether I'm genuinely open to being wrong, whether I'm listening to critics, and whether I'd be willing to change course if the evidence shifted. I think a person who does that and ends up having been wrong about the sign has still behaved well, and a person who gets lucky while reasoning sloppily has not. That's partly a coping mechanism, I'll admit. But I also think it's the right standard, because it's the only one that's actually actionable.

And then finally, I'd say there's something a bit self-undermining about treating "I'm uncertain whether this is good" as a reason to walk away from the thing you think is most important. The uncertainty is a reason to be humble, to prefer reversible actions, to diversify, to keep asking the question. It's not really a reason to go work on something where you've simply stopped asking. I'd much rather have thoughtful, worried people in this area than have them select themselves out because they couldn't guarantee the answer.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between being uncertain and having no reason to prefer one action over another. I’m very uncertain about the ultimate effects of almost anything you could do on a problem like AI. But that doesn’t mean I think all the options look equally good.

The case that seems compelling to me is: we could develop extraordinarily powerful AI systems, we don’t currently know how to make sure those systems behave as intended, and it would be good to understand that problem better before we’re facing it. That’s a reason to work on safety. It’s not a guarantee that any particular project with “safety” in its name is helpful. You still have to ask whether it’s actually making things safer, whether it might accelerate capabilities, and whether it might give people unjustified confidence.

So I wouldn’t frame the decision as, “Can I establish that my ultimate impact will be positive?” I’d frame it as, “What do I currently have the best reasons to believe will help, and how can I keep learning and correcting course?” You should take the possibility of doing harm seriously. But doing nothing is also a choice under uncertainty; it doesn’t give you a guaranteed neutral outcome.

r006.rationale: It gives a reason to work on AI safety while acknowledging uncertainty about ultimate effects and taking the possibility of harm seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish uncertainty about whether a problem is important from uncertainty about whether a particular thing you do is helpful. You could think that AI is going to be enormously consequential, and that there are very serious risks, without thinking that everything called “AI safety” is good to do.

So I wouldn’t make the decision at the level of, “I’ve chosen this cause, and now I’m going to push as hard as I can.” I’d ask: What’s the specific work? What’s the story for how it helps? What’s the story for how it could make things worse? And can I learn enough to distinguish those stories before making a big commitment?

The uncertainty is a reason to be careful, but it isn’t by itself a reason to stay out. Doing something else also has an uncertain impact, and not acting isn’t automatically neutral. You’re comparing options, all of which involve uncertainty.

For someone considering working on this, I think there’s a lot to be said for spending some time getting informed, finding people whose judgment you trust—including people who disagree with each other—and looking for work where you have a reasonably concrete account of why it helps. And then staying willing to change your mind. You don’t need confidence that your whole career will have a positive impact before taking a useful next step.
